'''''Narcissus asturiensis''''', the '''pygmy daffodil''',<ref>{{Cite web |title=Narcissus asturiensis (13) {{!}} pygmy daffodil Bulbs/RHS Gardening |url=http://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/11346/narcissus-asturiensis-(13)/details |access-date=2022-03-15 |website=www.rhs.org.uk |language=en-gb}}</ref> is a perennial [[bulb|bulbous plant]] native to the mountains of North Portugal and Spain, where it  grows at altitudes  up to 2000 m (6000 ft). {{As of|2022|March}}, [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|Kew]] sources consider the correct name to be '''''Narcissus cuneiflorus'''''.<ref name="POWO_65908-1">{{cite web |title=''Narcissus asturiensis'' (Jord.) Pugsley |work=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:65908-1 |access-date=2022-03-15 }}</ref><ref name="WCSP_282796">{{cite web |url=http://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do?name_id=282796 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190515110100/https://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do?name_id=282796 |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 15, 2019 |title=''Narcissus asturiensis'' |work=[[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]] (WCSP) |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] }}</ref>

This dwarf ''[[Narcissus (genus)|Narcissus]]'' is 7–12 cm (2.5– 5 in) tall and has small yellow flowers growing singly.

This is a threatened species in the wild, but it is amenable to cultivation.<ref name= santos>{{cite journal| last= Santos | first=  A. |author2=Fidalgo F. |author3=Santos I. |author4=Salema R.  | year=2002 | title=In vitro bulb formation of ''Narcissus asturiensis'', a threatened species of the Amaryllidaceae | journal= Journal of Horticultural Science & Biotechnology | volume=77 | issue= 2| pages=149–152  | doi= 10.1080/14620316.2002.11511471 | bibcode= 2002JHSB...77..149S | s2cid= 87286906 }}</ref>
It can be grown as a cold hardy garden plant, needing vernalization (a period of cold weather) in order to flower. As a garden plant, it will bloom in late January or early February at low altitudes.

This plant contains a number of [[alkaloid]]s including hemanthamine, hemanthidine,  tazettine and epimacronine.<ref name= lewis>{{cite journal| last=Lewis | first= John R. | year=  2000| title= Amaryllidaceae, muscarine, imidazole, oxazole, thiazole and peptide alkaloids, and other miscellaneous alkaloids | journal= Nat. Prod. Rep. | volume= 17 | issue= 1| pages=57–84  | url =http://www.rsc.org/ej/NP/2000/a809403i.pdf | doi = 10.1039/a809403i| pmid=10714899}}</ref>
